Reaching this stage does not, by itself, reproduce the full attack method or the cyber incidents previously reported. Several additional steps are required to chain vulnerabilities and achieve the resulting mass impact. Nevertheless, the fundamental milestone of circumventing the system’s authentication defenses has already been achieved.

This write-up aims to highlight a broader security concern: techniques that previously required highly specialized knowledge, substantial reverse-engineering expertise and potentially the collaboration of multiple individuals can increasingly be reproduced by leveraging publicly available CVE documentation, even when that documentation is incomplete or omits important implementation details.

Claroty’s experiment demonstrates that the AI agent initially struggled to reproduce the authentication bypass using the information and tools available in its initial investigation. However, Synacktiv’s publicly available 2023 advisory contained additional technical information concerning a similar authentication mechanism, the function. This raises an interesting research question: whether providing an AI model with previously published vulnerability research can substantially reduce the human intervention required to reproduce an analogous vulnerability in a newer product generation.

The implications extend well beyond the specific devices examined in this research. Many critical and operationally important environments rely on embedded controllers built around similar architectural principles. These include HVAC and building management systems, cold-chain logistics, pharmaceutical and hospital storage facilities, lighting and access control systems, elevators, water and wastewater pumping stations, EV chargers, solar inverters, and industrial process controllers.

Such systems frequently rely on embedded devices that may be remotely accessible, receive infrequent security updates, and remain operational long after their manufacturers have discontinued software maintenance.

items.title: GTA 6 Hits Massive $3.79 Billion In First-Day Sales
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI generated a record-breaking $3.79 billion in preorders and first-day sales, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive. The figure surpasses the lifetime global box-office earnings of Avengers: Endgame ($2.9 billion) and comes after more than a decade of development at a reported cost of $1.5 billion. The game developer declined to disclose the number of 'GTA 6' copies sold. 
"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI,'" Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you."
 
Further reading: Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait

items.title: Europe’s Democracy Is at Risk If It Cannot Control the AI It Depends On
items.author: Francesco Capria
items.content:
As Europe moves to make personal data easier to use for AI, its reliance on foreign models and infrastructure continues to grow. Cloud outages, restrictions on advanced AI systems, cyberattacks and experiments in political persuasion expose the risks of this dependence. The question is no longer just who will develop the most powerful AI, but whether Europe, and other democracies facing similar dependencies, can protect their economies, security and democratic institutions without relying on decisions made elsewhere.

The ambassadors of EU member states on 21 October 2026 agreed the negotiating position of the Council for the Digital Omnibus, the package with which the Commission wants to make European digital rules, including the GDPR, simpler. One of the provisions in it is about the use of personal data for training and operating artificial intelligence.

We are talking about one of the legal bases in Article 6 GDPR: . This means that personal data may be processed without consent, if it is necessary, and if the rights of the individuals involved are not infringed. This is not new; even as early as December 2024 the European Data Protection Board acknowledged that the legal basis of legitimate interest may, under certain conditions, allow the development and use of AI models. This is explicitly mentioned in a dedicated Council provision, though the Council clarifies that developing an AI system is not a legitimate interest in itself and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis. A key point is the right to object. After all, the Commission's November 2025 proposal included an unconditional right to object as one of the safeguards for AI. This right to object would have meant that data processing could be halted as soon as an objection was raised, but it was never implemented. This was later replaced by the Council with a reference to Article 21 GDPR, which allows individuals to object on certain grounds related to their situation. This means that if a company wants to develop an AI model, it must be able to prove either that there are compelling legitimate grounds that outweigh the interests, rights and freedoms of the individual, or that the data processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.

Provided they can be identified, it is possible to exclude data from objectors before training. However, it is very difficult to eliminate the influence of data used to train a large model in a verifiable way. This is called . There are techniques, but making sure they work without having to retrain the model from scratch is an open research question.

The new text of the Digital Omnibus is not yet law. The European Parliament still has to adopt its position, and only then will negotiations between the two institutions start. Understandably, the focus is very much on data for now. The Digital Omnibus could simplify the use of personal data covered by the GDPR for AI purposes. However, the key question remains: who has the means to transform that data into the most advanced models?

2. Who Controls AI Controls Progress

For the development of a state-of-the-art AI model, you need more and more computing power, energy and capital every year. According to Epoch AI, the research centre that collects data about the development of AI models, the computational power used to train the most advanced language models has increased about 5x per year since 2020. The cost of training state-of-the-art models has increased about 2.4x per year since 2016. But thanks to advances in algorithms, the computational power needed to reach the same result in the two language tests studied from 2012 to 2023 has been roughly cut in half every 8 months. So the resources needed to reach a certain performance level are becoming less and less. So we have two contradictory trends. It is becoming less computationally expensive to reach a level of performance that others have already reached, but to push the frontier further, you need more and more resources.

So looking at these two trends, if we analyse where the cutting-edge models are primarily being developed, we can see that it’s highly concentrated. According to the AI Index from Stanford, 50 significant models are attributed to the US in 2025, 30 to China, while in Europe it drops off sharply: only 2 models, one French, one British. It’s important to point out that this is an incomplete indicator because it’s the number of model releases and not the general technological capabilities of a country. But it’s a good indication of where the cutting-edge model development is most concentrated in the world.

The same report provides data that should prevent us from being too fatalistic. In March 2026, the best US model outperformed the Chinese model by only 2.7% in the Arena ranking, which is based on user preferences in direct comparisons of models. Even in February 2025, DeepSeek-R1, an model, was briefly as good as the best US model. This case shows that the gap is not fixed, even though it’s highly volatile. In fact, by March 2026, the gap between the best closed models and open models had increased from 0.5% in August 2024 to 3.3%. Six of the top ten models were closed.

But Europe isn’t sitting still. In June 2026, the Commission selected the EUROPA consortium, led by Italian company Domyn. The aim is to create a state-of-the-art, open-source European model in all 24 of the Union's official languages using public computing resources. As part of the Frontier AI Grand Challenge, the consortium can use up to 2.5% of the EuroHPC network's computing capacity for one year. The EuroHPC network is a European joint undertaking. However, as of November 2026, the model had not yet been released. On 30 July, they launched a call for proposals to set up to 7 ‘AI gigafactories’, i.e. large-scale computing centres for the training of advanced models. The deadline for applications for the largest facilities is 3 December 2026. For medium-sized facilities, the deadline has been extended to 4 February 2027, to allow time for member states to complete their budgetary procedures. Other organisations, like French company Mistral AI, are developing their own models and infrastructure. All of this is concrete progress in the right direction, but in my opinion, there’s room for discussion about the timing. The timing still lags behind the pace of the frontier: the gigafactory call is still open, while US investment is on a completely different scale.

3. The Day It All Switches Off

The ones who are most affected by the technological dependence on other countries are the users of the systems. Take Germany, for instance, the largest economy in the EU. The digital association Bitkom asked companies who they rely on: 71% of the 598 companies that use or evaluate cloud services cite American providers, while only 8% of the 589 companies for which the origin of the provider is important prefer American providers. And 85% of those surveyed believe that Germany is too dependent on US cloud providers. The picture is even clearer when it comes to AI: 76% of German companies that use it rely on ChatGPT, while Chinese models are virtually non-existent. Not a single company surveyed reported using Mistral. The president of Bitkom summarises the situation perfectly: the German economy is almost exclusively dependent on American AI applications.

You can only imagine what would happen if one of these services were to go down. Fortunately, we don’t have to imagine it. On 20 October 2025, a latent flaw in the system that automatically manages DNS records for DynamoDB (an AWS database) left the regional endpoint record empty for the service in the US-East-1 region of Amazon Web Services in Virginia. Hundreds of applications worldwide experienced disruptions of varying lengths; this included banking services and mobile network operators. Even Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine, announced it was down due to AWS issues. A single point of failure on the other side of the Atlantic literally paralysed operations that relied on that AWS region.

There are different types of failures. While the one we just saw was a technical one, on 12 June 2026, there was a political one. Just three days after revealing two configurations of the same frontier model, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, Anthropic received a directive from the US government on . They had to suspend access for all foreign nationals, both inside and outside the United States, including their own foreign employees. Anthropic couldn’t verify the nationality of the users in real time, so they had to deactivate the models for all customers to comply. The block was prompted by a report from Amazon researchers describing a way to bypass Fable 5’s safeguards, which Anthropic described as a borderline case of routine cyber defence work. According to The Next Web, it also put European access to the models through Project Glasswing in doubt. This made the issue significant enough for Brussels to discuss it directly with the White House, because getting access was via Washington. The restrictions were lifted on 30 June, meaning that Fable 5 has been available worldwide again since 1 July. However, Mythos 5 remains restricted to Glasswing partners.

There’s also a legal risk, that is intrinsically linked to the data risk. In June 2025, the director of public and legal affairs at Microsoft France appeared before the French Senate’s committee of inquiry on public procurement. He was asked a very specific question under oath: could he guarantee that the data of French citizens entrusted to Microsoft via the public procurement agency UGAP would never be passed on to the US authorities without the consent of the French authorities? Those unfamiliar with the issue might be surprised by the answer, but those in the know certainly won’t be. ‘I cannot guarantee that’, he said adding that it had never happened. This is because of the CLOUD Act, a US legislation that allows US authorities to request data held by a provider under their jurisdiction, even if it’s stored abroad.

These incidents show that services can be suspended for technical or political reasons. Even when everything is running smoothly, a US authority may order the handover of data stored abroad under the conditions set out in its own law. For data subject to the GDPR, that order alone doesn’t make the transfer lawful, and none of these factors are under the control of the European customer. They are powerless to prevent what happens on foreign infrastructure. Those who have not prepared a viable alternative can only watch and hope that the losses will be minimal.

4. Cybersecurity Moves at the Speed of Models

This is critically important in the field of cybersecurity, where both sides are already using state-of-the-art models.

In mid-September 2025, Anthropic discovered an espionage campaign, which it attributed, with a high level of confidence, to a group sponsored by the Chinese state. The hackers turned the company’s programming tool, Claude Code, into a quasi-autonomous agent. They used it to carry out reconnaissance, find vulnerabilities, write exploits, harvest credentials and move within networks. They targeted around thirty organisations, including large corporations, financial institutions, chemical companies and government agencies. In a small number of cases, the attacks were successful. This is, according to Anthropic, the first documented case of a large-scale attack, largely without human intervention during the operational phases.

However, these same capabilities can also be used defensively. Take Claude Mythos Preview, which was unveiled in April 2026, and which, according to Anthropic, identified thousands of serious vulnerabilities across all major operating systems and browsers. This was reserved for Project Glasswing and made available to around forty organisations that manage critical software, as well as around a dozen large American companies. Mozilla used a preliminary version of the model on Firefox’s code and was able to fix 271 vulnerabilities in a single release. Its chief technology officer stated that, for the first time, defenders had a clear chance of winning.

A more recent incident is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by much of the web, were discovered thanks to reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz. Wiz states that it also used GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. Wiz estimates that a researcher completed in one week a task that would have taken a team of experts months. Unfortunately, on 20 October 2026, the day before the patches were released, details were leaked, including a demonstration video that was mistakenly published and then removed. In the following days, the number of attack attempts increased from the thousands to the millions. The joint European advisory recommended assessing the need to isolate exposed applications where immediate patching was not possible, and governments in at least ten countries, including the Netherlands, France, Germany and Belgium, took the precaution of shutting down some of their web services. Hack the Box coined the term '' to describe this series of incidents. Wiz drew parallels between PHP2Shell and two of the most serious cybersecurity incidents to date: Heartbleed and Log4Shell. This was probably one of the most critical moments in cybersecurity, at least so far.

This trend in cybersecurity is not a recent discovery or a new development. As early as May 2025, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) predicted this in its assessment of the impact of AI up to 2027. The assessment noted that the time between the disclosure of a vulnerability and its exploitation had already been reduced to a matter of days, and that AI would almost certainly reduce this timeframe further. As universal access to AI for cyber defence by 2027 is considered a remote possibility, the gap between systems that can keep pace with potential AI-enhanced threats and those that cannot will continue to widen. The agency concluded that keeping pace with cutting-edge AI capabilities will be crucial for cyber resilience over the next decade.

If hospitals, electricity grids and banks rely on cutting-edge models for defence, the implication for Europe is clear: access to some of these tools depends on programmes run by American companies. This means that the security of European infrastructure increasingly depends on decisions taken elsewhere.

5. AI Enters the Ballot Box

There is also a far less visible risk that directly undermines the proper functioning of democracy.

On 4 December 2025, Nature and Science published two studies on the ability of chatbots to influence political opinions. The first study, led by Hause Lin and David Rand, involved conducting experiments during the 2024 US presidential election and the 2025 elections in Canada and Poland. Participants were made to converse for a few minutes with chatbots programmed to support one of the two main candidates. In Canada and Poland, on a scale of 0 to 100, the estimated difference in preference between groups assigned to chatbots supporting opposing candidates was around 10 points. In the United States, the effect was smaller but still greater than that estimated for traditional election adverts in previous studies, and around a third of this effect remained after a month. This figure does not indicate that 10% of voters changed their vote as a result of interacting with the dedicated chatbot; rather, it measures attitudes expressed in an experiment in which participants were aware that they were speaking to an AI. At the end of the conversation, they were informed that the model had been instructed to support a particular candidate. These results obviously pertain to these specific models and experiments and should not be generalised to other contexts.

The second study, published in Science, was conducted by the Oxford Internet Institute and the UK’s AI Security Institute. It involved nearly 77,000 participants, 19 language models and 707 political issues. In this case, the chatbots were made more persuasive mainly by post-training and the instructions they received rather than by the size of the models or the personalisation of the messages. Their persuasive power was strongly associated with the number of verifiable claims: the models were more convincing when they underpinned their arguments with factual claims. However, the same factors that increased persuasiveness also led to an increase in inaccurate claims.

This is linked to a well-known problem in the field: ‘, or the tendency of AI models to tell users what they want to hear. This behaviour largely comes from the way AI models are trained: when people rate answers, they tend to prefer the ones that agree with them, and the models learn to do the same. A 2023 study by Anthropic found this behaviour in five widely used AI assistants, which sometimes chose agreeable but incorrect answers over correct ones. The most notable example occurred in April 2025, when OpenAI withdrew a GPT-4o update after admitting that it had made the model 'noticeably more sycophantic'.

Persuasion and sycophancy are two sides of the same coin. In persuasion, the model directs the interlocutor towards a particular argument, whereas in sycophancy, it goes along with them. However, in both cases, when the aim is to optimise the person’s reaction rather than the truth of what is said, accuracy becomes a cost. This interpretation should be taken as such, but it is consistent with these findings.

But what impact does all this have outside the laboratory? A 2026 study co-authored by some of the researchers behind the Science paper found that people were up to 20 percentage points more likely to sign a real petition (providing a name and email address) after a persuasive conversation with an AI than those who had discussed a neutral topic. When comparing the different experimental conditions, the authors found no significant correlation between the effects on opinions and signatures. Changing someone’s opinion and getting them to take action are two different things, and the actual effect on voting behaviour remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the use of these systems has increased over the past year. According to the Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report, the weekly use of chatbots to obtain news rose, on average, across the 48 markets examined, from 7% to 10% in one year. Among 18–24-year-olds, it reached 17%. However, the quality of responses remains an issue. A study led by the BBC and the European Broadcasting Union found that 45% of the answers provided by chatbots on current affairs contained at least one significant error.

These findings pose a problem for democratic debate.A system used by millions of people does not need to lie to spread propaganda or shape public perception. All it takes is choosing the right sources, highlighting the right arguments, leaving out conflicting ones and confirming what the user already believes. This is an enormous amount of power, and it is controlled by those who decide how the models are trained. Today, these decisions are taken by a handful of private entities, almost all of which are based outside Europe. Meanwhile, public scrutiny of how accurate, persuasive or sycophantic their models are remains sporadic. No democracy should allow the way its citizens are informed and make decisions to be left to the goodwill of a few companies.

So far, everything we have considered relates to existing technologies, but we will soon have to address how all the issues raised will be managed with the advent of artificial general intelligence (AGI), although we have yet to decide what would constitute proof of its arrival. Experts can give very different answers on this point.

In 2025, a group of 33 researchers, including Yoshua Bengio, proposed a measurable definition of AGI as a system that equals or exceeds the cognitive competence and versatility of a well-educated adult. They identified ten areas, including reasoning, knowledge, memory and perception. Using this yardstick, GPT-4 achieved 27% of the expected score in the third version of the study, while GPT-5 achieved 57%. The models demonstrated extensive knowledge of what they had learnt during training in the tests described by the authors, but one of the greatest difficulties arose when they had to learn new information and retrieve it in a subsequent session without the use of external tools. Therefore, 57% reflects a highly uneven profile of capabilities and does not provide a precise estimate of how long it will take to achieve AGI.

OpenAI uses a different metric, which is more based on work. In its charter, OpenAI states that AGI is “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. The metric is different because of ‘autonomy’. If you give the system a task of finding a computer fault, then it could be told that once the technician has all the evidence, it should come up with the cause. Taking the initial report, identifying the fault, fixing it and verifying that the solution is effective is a much larger task, and above all, an independent one. OpenAI’s metric is about how much the system can do autonomously. METR measures exactly this: the length of the tasks that models can complete independently has doubled roughly every seven months between 2019 and 2025.

Another point of view is that some form of general intelligence already exists. In a commentary in Nature in February 2026, Eddy Keming Chen and three colleagues at the University of California, San Diego, argued that certain models already show the flexibility we associate with human intelligence. They argue this because a person can be competent in reasoning in various domains, yet still make mistakes and need assistance. So the same standard, they argue, should apply to machines. This is a clear and strong position on the debate, but it shows that making any proclamation or ruling out the arrival of AGI without defining the standard by which we recognise it makes no sense.

No one knows when it will arrive, how it will arrive, what it will mean, whether it will be conscious or have emotions. These are more philosophical than technical questions. What we can reasonably expect is that the first to have it will have unprecedented power in human history. Clearly, if it were an American company that developed such a system, it would be bound by US laws. This would lead to things like export controls that temporarily prevented the use of Fable 5, or the need to share data with US authorities. Microsoft admitted to the French Senate that it cannot rule out such requests. But let’s imagine, although we don’t really need to anymore, that this kind of intelligence is essential for research, healthcare, economy, public administration and defence. Europe would be completely dependent on technologies from elsewhere with no alternatives, and would have little to say about the rules. This is a clear structural dependency and weakness that would undermine democracy, as we discussed before, but on a much larger scale. If you make it easier to use personal data to build AI systems, without at the same time decreasing the dependence of Europe on models and infrastructure from elsewhere, you risk making this imbalance even worse, which might be hard to solve when even more advanced technologies arrive.

7. Europe’s Plan B - Test It Out

One way to assess Europe's autonomy would be to ask those who run essential services simple questions: what would they do if the AI model on which their systems depend suddenly became unavailable or unreliable for any reason? How long would it take them to get their systems back up to full operational capacity? What activities could still be done? These questions highlight three key issues that could potentially expand the scope of the instruments set out in European legislation.

First, you need to ensure business continuity. There’s already a precedent for this in the financial sector. Article 28 of the DORA Regulation states that financial entities must have exit strategies for IT services that support essential or important functions. These plans must be documented, properly tested and regularly reviewed. The NIS2 Directive also includes measures for business continuity for the relevant entities. And in July 2026, the European Commission’s guidelines on the resilience of critical entities explicitly recommended that it should be possible to still operate manually in case of failure of automated or AI-based systems. So the idea would be to make these checks explicit for the individual AI models used in essential functions of key services like healthcare, energy and public administration, as well as for the dependence on their suppliers. For example, if a bank is using a model to help the staff detect fraud, then during a drill, they should be able to turn off the model and use an alternative procedure to check things, in order to measure how it affects the time and accuracy of fraud detection.

The second issue is cybersecurity. The Cyber Solidarity Act created a pool of incident response services that are managed by ENISA. These services are provided by selected operators. Also, the same regulation includes a network of national and cross-border centres that can use AI tools to detect and analyse cyber threats. These would need to be complemented by a common , available to authorised teams and tested in advance in joint exercises. This would allow you to know in advance what tasks can be performed by this model and what still requires a specialist’s intervention. Such a model could build on the technology capabilities developed in projects like EUROPA and future gigafactories, but it would need to be adapted for cybersecurity purposes and be updated regularly, with dedicated computing resources, and tested regularly to make sure it works.

The third issue is directly related to the proper functioning of a democracy, namely the right of citizens to know how they’re being informed. In the AI Act, providers of general-purpose models that pose a systemic risk are required to assess their own models. There’s already an independent scientific panel, as defined in the regulation. A similar precedent exists in the Digital Services Act, which requires very large online platforms and search engines to undergo independent audits at least once a year, and the reports must be made public. But there is no general requirement to assess the persuasiveness or sycophancy of chatbots. There is a lack of a system of regular independent audits of the most commonly used chatbots in Europe, using comparable methods and making the results public. This would allow citizens to know the accuracy, sycophancy and persuasiveness of the systems they use. For example, to measure sycophancy, you could ask the same questions repeatedly, but with false premises to see if it corrects them. To measure persuasiveness, you could compare how opinions change after different conversations with consenting volunteers.

None of these suggestions assume that Europe needs to overtake the US or China in developing cutting-edge models. It’s about reducing the dependence on individual suppliers, and showing that essential services can still function even if a particular model is unavailable. As we saw from the Stanford data, the technical gap can be reduced, and we’ve already taken the first steps. The question of who controls the technology is still unanswered. The answer also depends on the choices Europe makes today. It makes sense to make it easier to use data for AI, but only if we also invest in the ability to develop and use this technology here, without necessarily having to rely on foreign suppliers.

Although this article focuses on Europe, the problem extends far beyond its borders. Any democracy that relies on technology controlled elsewhere must ask itself a fundamental question: how much autonomy can it afford to surrender? items.title: What Should Undo Do After a List Has Moved?
items.author: di wu
items.content:
Alder, Birch, and Cedar are three cards in a reading list. Delete Birch and an Undo button appears. Before pressing it, move Cedar to the top. Where should Birch go when you bring it back? This tiny sequence exposes a product decision that is easy to bury in an array operation.

Start by recording the index. Birch was at index one. After the move, the list reads Cedar, Alder, so inserting at index one gives Cedar, Birch, Alder. That is a perfectly defensible result if the promise is “restore the second slot.” Someone who remembers placing Birch just after Alder may find it surprising.

Try a different promise. On deletion, remember the IDs of the neighbours along with the deleted card and its ID. On restore, look for the former preceding neighbour first. If Alder survives, place Birch immediately after it. The result in our example is Cedar, Alder, Birch. Giving precedence to the preceding neighbour is an explicit choice. Both old neighbors are still present, but their order has reversed. There is no slot between them that preserves both old relationships.

Now, delete Alder before hitting Undo. The preceding neighbor is gone, so try the former following neighbor and restore Birch immediately before Cedar. If both neighbors have gone, append Birch. For a list sorted by an independent field such as a due date, a different rule makes sense: restore the record and let the sorter decide its position.

Test one more interruption. Another tab restores Birch while the banner is still on screen. Pressing Undo again should leave the list exactly as it stands. Check for the restored card by stable ID before inserting it. Two cards can have the same title. A title check can accidentally suppress a legitimate restoration, and a length check can miss a pair of cards in the wrong order.

A small test can exercise these decisions without opening a browser. Begin with the three IDs, perform the delete and move, then restore twice. Compare the complete sequence after each restore. Run a second case with the preceding neighbor removed. Those two examples give the person writing the button label something concrete to describe, and the next maintainer a way to tell which ordering changes are intentional.

This is an AI-generated design exercise. The cards and interactions are illustrative.

items.title: We Tested Every REST Endpoint and Missed the Queue That Dropped $62K
items.author: Akhil
items.content:
{
  "Attributes": {
    "ApproximateNumberOfMessages": "4819",
    "ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible": "0"
  }
}

That was the output of aws sqs get-queue-attributes on prod-merchant-payouts-dlq when our finance lead finally asked why Tuesday's Stripe Connect batch was missing in disbursements.

Every single REST API contract test in our monorepo had passed that morning. Our Playwright suite was green. Our Go service's unit tests were green. Our TypeScript worker's unit tests were green.

None of them caught the bug, because the bug did not live on an HTTP route. It lived in the invisible gap between a Go service calling and a Node.js worker calling JSON.parse(record.Body) as PayoutRequestedEvent.

Why REST Contract Tests Miss Half Your Architecture

Engineering teams spend huge amounts of energy locking down synchronous HTTP boundaries. We generate TypeScript clients from OpenAPI specs, run Supertest against Express routers, and fail CI if a response field changes from to .

Then we take an asynchronous SQS queue, a Kafka topic, or an internal SNS fan-out—which often carries the actual money-moving side effects—and treat it like a lawless JSON dropbox.

In our case, two separate teams owned the two ends of :

  • ): Maintained by the core billing team in Go.
  • ): Maintained by the platform team in TypeScript/Node 22.

In , the consumer had a type annotation that looked safe in code review and meant literally nothing at runtime:

// Looks typed in your IDE. Completely unchecked at runtime.
const payload = JSON.parse(message.Body!) as {
  merchantId: string;
  payoutCents: number;
  currency: string;
};

When refactored its decimal serialization to avoid float rounding and started emitting as a string instead of as an integer, happily returned a string. Downstream, Math.round(payload.payoutCents) did not throw—Wait: actually, works in JavaScript!

What throw was the strict Postgres / Stripe SDK validation two functions later (Invalid integer: "14900.00" when a fractional fee was included), crashing the worker, exhausting , and dumping 4,819 messages into prod-merchant-payouts-dlq.

Nobody was watching the DLQ metric in Datadog because that queue had sat at for eight months.

What Unit Tests Lied About on Both Sides

When we pulled the two repos side-by-side after replaying the DLQ, both teams had written tests for that exact flow:

  • asserted that its helper produced valid JSON containing . It passed.
  • had a Jest test with a hardcoded fixture file fixtures/payout-message.json where was still . It passed too.

Static fixtures in consumer unit tests are a slow-acting poison. The day you write fixtures/payout-message.json, it matches reality. Six months later, after three producer refactors, your consumer tests are certifying a payload shape that no longer exists anywhere in production.

One Shared JSON Schema Contract That Breaks Both Repos.

We did not want to deploy a heavy Confluent Schema Registry just for 14 SQS queues. We wanted something boring that worked across Go and TypeScript inside GitHub Actions with zero new infrastructure.

So we made JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) the single source of truth inside a lightweight shared directory (contracts/queues/*.schema.json), paired with:

  1. Runtime validation at the consumer boundary using (or compiled to JSON Schema) so malformed messages fail at line 1 of the handler with a structured log instead of half-way through a Stripe call.
  2. A CI cross-repo contract check so if changes a struct tag or field type, it has to run against the exact same file that consumes.

Here is contracts/queues/payout-requested.v1.schema.json:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "$id": "https://contracts.internal/queues/payout-requested.v1.schema.json",
  "type": "object",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "required": ["eventId", "merchantId", "payoutCents", "currency", "occurredAt"],
  "properties": {
    "eventId": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },
    "merchantId": { "type": "string", "minLength": 4 },
    "payoutCents": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1 },
    "currency": { "type": "string", "enum": ["USD", "EUR", "GBP"] },
    "occurredAt": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" }
  }
}

And here is the TypeScript consumer boundary wrapper (src/queues/validateMessage.ts) that replaced :

import Ajv from 'ajv';
import addFormats from 'ajv-formats';
import payoutSchema from '../../contracts/queues/payout-requested.v1.schema.json';

const ajv = new Ajv({ allErrors: true, strict: true });
addFormats(ajv);

const validatePayout = ajv.compile<{
  eventId: string;
  merchantId: string;
  payoutCents: number;
  currency: 'USD' | 'EUR' | 'GBP';
  occurredAt: string;
}>(payoutSchema);

export function parsePayoutMessage(rawBody: string | undefined) {
  if (!rawBody) {
    throw new Error('SQS_EMPTY_BODY: Missing message body');
  }

  const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(rawBody);
  if (!validatePayout(parsed)) {
    const details = ajv.errorsText(validatePayout.errors);
    throw new Error(`SCHEMA_DRIFT_ERROR: ${details}`);
  }

  return parsed;
}

Notice additionalProperties: false and on . If ever serializes as a string again, rejects it in under 0.1 milliseconds with an unmistakable instead of letting it corrupt downstream state.

Testing the Real SQS Loop With LocalStack in CI.

Validating a schema in memory is only half the story. You also want to prove that the Go producer's survive SQS attributes, base64/JSON encoding, and the TypeScript consumer's function.

We added a 55-line integration test (tests/contracts/sqs-payout-contract.test.ts) that spins up LocalStack via Testcontainers (or a GitHub Actions service container), runs the Go producer binary's command to push real messages onto a local queue, and lets the TypeScript consumer pull and validate them:

import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';
import { SQSClient, CreateQueueCommand, ReceiveMessageCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sqs';
import { parsePayoutMessage } from '../../src/queues/validateMessage';

const sqs = new SQSClient({
  region: 'us-east-1',
  endpoint: process.env.LOCALSTACK_URL || 'http://127.0.0.1:4566',
  credentials: { accessKeyId: 'test', secretAccessKey: 'test' },
});

test('Go producer payload passes TypeScript SQS consumer contract', async () => {
  const { QueueUrl } = await sqs.send(
    new CreateQueueCommand({ QueueName: `payouts-contract-${Date.now()}` })
  );

  // Run the actual Go producer serialization path against LocalStack
  execFileSync('./bin/ledger-emit-sample', ['--queue-url', QueueUrl!], {
    env: { ...process.env, AWS_ENDPOINT_URL: process.env.LOCALSTACK_URL || 'http://127.0.0.1:4566' },
  });

  const received = await sqs.send(
    new ReceiveMessageCommand({
      QueueUrl,
      MaxNumberOfMessages: 1,
      WaitTimeSeconds: 3,
    })
  );

  expect(received.Messages).toHaveLength(1);
  const validated = parsePayoutMessage(received.Messages![0].Body);
  expect(validated.payoutCents).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});

That single test runs in in GitHub Actions. No mocked JSON fixtures. If a Go developer changes to on —even by adding to a Go struct tag—that test blows up on their PR before ever sees it in production.

Never Let a Dead-Letter Queue Sit Silent Again

The other embarrassing half of the $62K incident was not technical—it was operational. A queue had 4,819 failed payout messages sitting in it for 19 hours because nobody had wired an alarm to ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible > 0 on .

We fixed that across all 14 queues in one Terraform module (infra/modules/sqs_dlq_alarm/main.tf) so every new queue gets a PagerDuty/Slack alert on in the DLQ, not message #4,819:

resource "aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm" "dlq_not_empty" {
  for_each            = toset(var.dlq_names)
  alarm_name          = "${each.value}-has-messages"
  comparison_operator = "GreaterThanThreshold"
  evaluation_periods  = 1
  metric_name         = "ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible"
  namespace           = "AWS/SQS"
  period              = 60
  statistic           = "Maximum"
  threshold           = 0
  treat_missing_data  = "notBreaching"

  dimensions = {
    QueueName = each.value
  }

  alarm_actions = [var.ops_alerts_sns_topic_arn]
}

Zero tolerance on DLQ depth sounds aggressive until you realize a dead-letter queue is literally a bucket of failed customer promises. If one message lands there, you want to know within 60 seconds, not when finance reconciles Stripe payouts on Wednesday morning.

Handling In-Flight Messages During Schema Upgrades

Putting a strict JSON Schema validator on a queue consumer introduces a subtle trap during rolling deployments: .

When Kubernetes rolls to a new version, there can easily be 800 messages still sitting in SQS serialized by the version of . If you rename a required field or tighten an enum in payout-requested.v1.schema.json, your new consumer pods will immediately reject valid in-flight messages as .

We learned that the hard way on our second schema update. Now we enforce two rules in CI:

  1. schema in a breaking way. Adding an optional property is fine. Removing a field, changing a type, or adding a new key means creating payout-requested.v2.schema.json and supporting both and in the consumer until traffic drains to zero.
  2. Automate the backwards-compatibility check. We added a 45-line CI script (scripts/check-schema-backcompat.ts) that diffs every modified file against and fails the PR if a field was added or a property's changed:
import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';
import fs from 'node:fs';

interface JsonSchema {
  required?: string[];
  properties?: Record<string, { type?: string }>;
}

const changedFiles = execFileSync(
  'git',
  ['diff', '--name-only', 'origin/main...HEAD', '--', 'contracts/queues/*.schema.json'],
  { encoding: 'utf8' }
)
  .trim()
  .split('\n')
  .filter(Boolean);

for (const file of changedFiles) {
  let oldRaw = '';
  try {
    oldRaw = execFileSync('git', ['show', `origin/main:${file}`], { encoding: 'utf8' });
  } catch {
    // Brand new schema version (e.g., v2) — always allowed
    continue;
  }

  const prev = JSON.parse(oldRaw) as JsonSchema;
  const next = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8')) as JsonSchema;

  const prevReq = new Set(prev.required || []);
  for (const key of next.required || []) {
    if (!prevReq.has(key)) {
      console.error(`BREAKING: Added required field "${key}" to ${file}. Bump to a new version instead.`);
      process.exit(1);
    }
  }

  for (const [prop, def] of Object.entries(prev.properties || {})) {
    const nextDef = next.properties?.[prop];
    if (!nextDef || nextDef.type !== def.type) {
      console.error(`BREAKING: Property "${prop}" changed or removed in ${file}. Bump schema version.`);
      process.exit(1);
    }
  }
}

console.log('All modified queue schemas are backwards-compatible.');

Replaying 4,819 Dead-Letter Messages Without Double-Paying

One last thing nobody tells you until you actually have to drain a 4,819-message financial DLQ: you cannot just click "Start DLQ Redrive" in the AWS Console and walk away.

During the 19-hour outage, our finance team had already manually wired payouts for 140 urgent enterprise merchants via the Stripe dashboard. If we had blindly redriven all 4,819 messages back into the main queue, those 140 merchants would have been paid twice.

Before replaying a single message, we added an INSERT INTO processed_queue_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING idempotency guard backed by Postgres, pre-seeded it with the 140 manually settled s, and ran a small redrive script that patched from string to integer on the fly while logging every skipped duplicate.

We tested the redrive script with on the first 50 DLQ messages, verified the Stripe idempotency keys matched, and then drained the remaining 4,769 messages in batches of 100. The whole replay finished in 4 minutes and 40 seconds across 20 concurrent workers, with zero double payouts and zero manual spreadsheet reconciliation afterward.

That idempotency table stayed in permanently—because SQS is at-least-once delivery anyway, and sooner or later every distributed queue delivers the same message twice.

The Quiet Side Effect Nobody Mentions

Once we put JSON Schema contracts and LocalStack round-trip tests on our SQS queues, we expected fewer production outages. And yes, we have had schema-drift DLQ incidents in the five months since.

What surprised me was how much faster onboarding got. New engineers stopped having to through three Go repositories to figure out what shape an SQS event actually had—they just opened contracts/queues/*.schema.json and read the exact contract in ten seconds.

If your test suite checks every REST route twice while your SQS, Kafka, or BullMQ workers still rely on JSON.parse(...) as MyType and hand-written test fixtures, you are only testing half your system. The other half is one struct tag away from a very quiet, very expensive pileup.

items.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports: Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly.
 
[...] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.

items.title: The Anchor Effect: Why Destination Footfall Doesn't Equal Retail Demand
items.author: Dmitry Poroshin
items.content:
1. The 50-Million-Visitor Metric

On 30 September 2026, Battersea Power Station's developers announced its 50-millionth visitor since the restored landmark opened in October 2022.

The milestone signals destination appeal, not shopfront footfall. It is neither a count of unique customers nor evidence of how visitors move or what they intend to buy.

Here, an is a major district destination, not a conventional shopping-centre tenant. Its benefit depends on visitor routes and spending.

2. Spatial Divergence in Master-Planned Estates

Source: Wandsworth Council, Table 41; survey: 3 October–7 November 2025.

Vacancy ranges from 6% to 38%. Table 41 covers 148 units in completed zones; the report refers to around 150 across the wider development. It records occupancy, not why units were vacant.

The datasets cover different periods (the survey was in autumn 2025; the visitor milestone was announced in September 2026) and establish no link between visits and vacancy. Vacancy may also reflect rents, unit size, lease terms or fit-out.

3. From Destination Traffic to Storefront Exposure

A destination visitor does not necessarily pass every unit, notice its frontage, enter, or buy. The path to purchase has five stages:

This is a conceptual measurement chain, not a funnel measured at Battersea.

  1. People entering the development.
  2. The paths they use.
  3. Passages within a shopfront's visible approach area.
  4. Passers-by crossing the threshold.
  5. Visitors completing a purchase.

The stages are not interchangeable: destination visits are not frontage footfall, and frontage footfall is not sales. A side-street shop may receive less traffic than one on the main boulevard, even near the same station. Test this with network analysis and observed counts.

4. Proximity, Accessibility, and Exposure

These measures answer different spatial questions:

Euclidean buffer - How close is the unit in a straight line?

Network isochrone - How easily can pedestrians reach it?

Frontage flow and visibility - How many people pass the shopfront?

uses a Euclidean buffer, such as a 300-metre circle. It gives a quick overview but ignores railway lines, buildings and inaccessible entrances.

uses a network isochrone: the area reachable within a given time along pedestrian paths. A five-minute isochrone measures reachability, not movement; quiet and busy streets may lie within the same area.

is pedestrian flow past a frontage and the opportunity to see it. It depends on route choice, entrance position, barriers and sightlines. Network and origin-destination models estimate routes, not actual frontage flow; observed counts or validated mobility data are needed.

Two units may both be 150 metres' walk from a station. is visible from the main route to nearby offices; is behind a corner. Their isochrones may match, but A could receive more pass-by exposure. Counts establish the difference.

5. Matching Pedestrian Flow to the Occupier's P&L

Footfall has no universal commercial value: its importance depends on the tenant's business model, opening hours and customer behavior.

A simplified revenue model is:

Estimated Revenue = Catchment Footfall × Frontage Capture Rate × Store Entry Rate × Purchase Conversion × Average Transaction Value

The variables represent catchment volume, frontage capture, entry, purchase conversion and average spend. Use a consistent period; if footfall is counted at the shopfront, omit the first two stages. This estimates sales, not profit.

Connecting revenue to occupancy costs

OCR = Occupancy Costs/Store Revenue × 100%

The Occupancy Cost Ratio compares revenue with rent and defined property charges, such as service charges. Use consistent cost definitions and revenue excluding VAT.

High exposure does not guarantee viability. If occupancy costs exceed what achievable revenue can support, the tenant may struggle. OCR is not profitability-gross margin, staffing and other expenses still matter-but it links location quality to the cost of securing it.

Different retail formats, different flow profiles

  • Commuters may help, but offices, homes, leisure destinations and repeat customers also drive demand.
  • Lunch and evening patterns may matter more than daily totals; offices, residents and leisure uses contribute at different times.
  • Specialist and appointment-led retail: Showrooms may rely on planned visits and referrals rather than walk-ins; accessibility may matter more than passing footfall.

An anchor can generate complementary demand or retain spending in its own restaurants, cafés and shops. The effect depends on tenant category, routes and overlap between offers.

6. A Diagnostic Framework for Retail Site Selection.

Move from broad context to unit-level evidence:

  1. Define the unit and catchment: frontage, entrances, nearby destinations and target customers.
  2. Map the pedestrian network: streets, crossings, station exits, restrictions and barriers.
  3. Assess routes and visibility: likely origins, destinations and sightlines; validate modelled routes.
  4. pedestrian counts or privacy-compliant mobility data across times, weekdays, weekends and seasons.
  5. establish whether nearby uses complement or compete with the proposed business.
  6. estimate revenue, calculate OCR and compare it with gross margin, rent, service charges, staffing and fit-out costs. Test downside and upside scenarios.

A single footfall score cannot capture the commercial case. Identify the assumptions driving the result and the evidence supporting them.

7. What Public Data Can and Cannot Tell Us

Public data provides a starting point, not the final answer.

show destination activity, not movement between zones, repeat visits, or traffic at a particular unit. Check the counting methodology before treating a milestone as a unique-visitor figure.

, such as Wandsworth Council's survey, provide occupancy and commercial-use information, not reasons for vacancy, store sales, conversion rates or lease terms.

from TfL Open Data and its API portal help establish accessibility. Station-level passenger data does not measure pedestrian movement along individual streets or shopfronts.

Combine planning and occupancy records, transport and pedestrian-network data, privacy-compliant mobility data, frontage counts and tenant assumptions.

For an individual Battersea unit, these sources cannot show which routes carry the most pedestrians or count shopfront passers-by. That requires geocoded entrances, route analysis and observed or validated flow data. Accessibility maps are not footfall maps.

8. Conclusion: Measure the Demand That Reaches the Door

Battersea's visitor milestone and Wandsworth Council's survey describe different aspects of the development: destination activity and vacancy across completed zones. Neither explains an individual unit's performance.

Proximity, accessibility and exposure must be kept separate. A unit can be close to an attraction but poorly positioned on pedestrian routes, easy to reach but receive little spontaneous traffic, or busy yet fail to attract customers suited to the tenant's offer.

Connect spatial evidence to observed movement and store economics: estimate frontage flow, model sales conversion and test whether revenue supports occupancy costs. That is the difference between measuring destination activity and assessing a retail location.

items.title: We Killed Our Staging Environment and Moved QA to Production Canaries
items.author: Akhil
items.content:
At 11:40 AM on a Monday, nine engineers were sitting in a Slack thread watching a progress bar that had not moved in 45 minutes.

Someone had merged a half-baked Alembic migration into and locked the table. Meanwhile, a real bug on was actively hitting paying customers in production, and our hotfix could not ship because company policy said every release had to pass a full QA sign-off on staging first.

Four hours later, the hotfix finally went out. Nobody felt safer. Worse, when we checked our incident log that week, we noticed something embarrassing: staging had failed to catch four of our last five production outages anyway.

Why? Because staging had 120 clean seed rows in Postgres, zero concurrent webhook traffic from Stripe, and a Redis instance that never evicted a key. Production had 18 million rows, spiky Monday morning batch jobs, and weird legacy payloads from 2021.

We were paying in AWS bills to test against a fantasy world.

Two months later, we turned off the shared staging cluster for good.

Why Shared Staging Always Turns Into a Bottleneck

If your team has more than five developers, a shared staging environment rots in predictable ways:

  • Developer A runs a destructive migration for Feature X; Developer B's API tests immediately fail for reasons that have nothing to do with their branch.
  • Someone manually edits a feature flag or deletes a test tenant during a demo, and three automated suites go red until someone resets the database.
  • Queries that finish in 4 milliseconds on 120 staging rows do a full sequential scan and time out at 30 seconds against 18 million production rows.

We still run fast unit tests, contract checks, and ephemeral per-PR Docker Compose smoke tests in GitHub Actions (those cost us about $410/month now). What we killed was the long-lived, shared "pre-production gate" where QA engineers spent half their week babysitting stale seed data.

Instead, we moved real verification into production behind three guardrails: progressive traffic splitting, dark-launch shadow traffic, and isolated synthetic probes.

Guardrail 1: Argo Rollouts With Automated Prometheus Rollbacks

If you test in production without automatic blast-radius control, you are not doing shift-right testing—you are just breaking things faster.

We replaced our standard Kubernetes manifests with . When a new container image ships, it gets for three minutes. An polls Prometheus every 30 seconds. If the 5xx error rate crosses 0.5% or p99 latency jumps above 650ms, Argo aborts the rollout and drains the canary pods in about 45 seconds without a human touching anything.

Here is the exact and pair we use for our service:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: canary-slo-check
spec:
  args:
    - name: service-name
  metrics:
    - name: http-5xx-rate
      interval: 30s
      failureLimit: 2
      successCondition: result[0] <= 0.005
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service-name}}",status=~"5.."}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service-name}}"}[2m]))
    - name: p99-latency-ms
      interval: 30s
      failureLimit: 2
      successCondition: result[0] <= 650
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="{{args.service-name}}"}[2m])) by (le)) * 1000
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: exports-api
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 3m }
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: canary-slo-check
            args:
              - name: service-name
                value: exports-api-canary
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: canary-slo-check
            args:
              - name: service-name
                value: exports-api-canary
        - setWeight: 100

Notice the two separate pauses: 3 minutes at 5% traffic, then 5 minutes at 25%. Most memory leaks and bad database query plans show up right around the 25% mark when connection pools start filling up.

Guardrail 2: Shadow Traffic for Risky Read and Pricing Paths

Canaries are great, but what if you rewrote a pricing calculator or a search query planner and do not want to see a wrong number?

For read-only and idempotent endpoints, we mirror live production HTTP requests to the new version in the background using Envoy/Nginx traffic shadowing. The user gets the response from the old stable pods. Meanwhile, the canary pod processes the exact same real-world JSON payload, headers, and edge-case query strings—and we compare the status codes and latency in Datadog.

Here is the Nginx Ingress annotation block we used before migrating to Envoy:

location /api/v1/pricing/quote {
    proxy_pass http://pricing_stable;
    mirror /_shadow_pricing;
    mirror_request_body on;
}

location = /_shadow_pricing {
    internal;
    proxy_pass http://pricing_canary$request_uri;
    proxy_set_header X-Shadow-Traffic "true";
    proxy_connect_timeout 200ms;
    proxy_read_timeout 500ms;
}

Two hard-won lessons on shadow traffic:

  1. or endpoints unless your downstream handler checks and skips writing to Stripe or sending customer emails. We learned to put an explicit middleware guard at the top of our Express router that rejects on non-GET routes unless the handler opts in.
  2. Set aggressive timeouts (). Nginx's directive sends the subrequest asynchronously, so a slow canary does not normally block the user, if you exhaust worker connections during a spike. Short timeouts keep the shadow pool from starving the primary pool.

Shadow traffic caught a bug in our search query builder that staging never saw in three weeks: real customers were passing 40+ comma-separated filter tags in a single URL, blowing past an internal regex limit and throwing errors.

Guardrail 3: Tenant-Isolated Synthetic Probes in Production

Shadow traffic tests existing endpoints, and canaries test real user flows. Neither one tests a brand-new multi-step workflow (like onboarding a new workspace or generating a PDF export) before you flip the feature flag on for customers.

That is where our synthetic canary probe comes in.

We created one dedicated internal tenant in production (tenant_id: "canary_synthetic_01"), excluded from all revenue and analytics rollups in Snowflake. Every 60 seconds, a lightweight Kubernetes runs a Playwright/API probe against production with .

If we are rolling out a new billing flow behind a LaunchDarkly/Unleash feature flag, we turn that flag on for first. The probe exercises the real production database, real Redis cluster, and real S3 bucket—then cleans up its own test artifacts at the end of the run.

Here is the TypeScript probe script () that runs on that 60-second loop:

import { strict as assert } from 'node:assert';

const PROD_BASE_URL = process.env.PROD_BASE_URL || 'https://api.example.com';
const CANARY_TOKEN = process.env.CANARY_SYNTHETIC_TOKEN!;

async function runCanaryProbe() {
  const start = Date.now();

  // 1. Trigger a real export job under the isolated synthetic tenant
  const createRes = await fetch(`${PROD_BASE_URL}/api/v1/exports`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${CANARY_TOKEN}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'x-canary-probe': 'true',
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      format: 'csv',
      dateRangeDays: 7,
    }),
  });

  assert.equal(createRes.status, 202, `Expected 202 from /exports, got ${createRes.status}`);
  const { exportId } = (await createRes.json()) as { exportId: string };

  // 2. Poll until the worker finishes or 15s budget expires
  let status = 'pending';
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 15; attempt++) {
    const pollRes = await fetch(`${PROD_BASE_URL}/api/v1/exports/${exportId}`, {
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${CANARY_TOKEN}`,
        'x-canary-probe': 'true',
      },
    });
    assert.equal(pollRes.status, 200, `Poll failed with ${pollRes.status}`);
    const data = (await pollRes.json()) as { status: string; downloadUrl?: string };
    status = data.status;

    if (status === 'completed') {
      assert.ok(data.downloadUrl, 'Completed export missing S3 downloadUrl');
      break;
    }
    if (status === 'failed') {
      throw new Error(`Export job ${exportId} failed in production worker`);
    }
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000));
  }

  assert.equal(status, 'completed', `Export ${exportId} timed out in status=${status}`);

  // 3. Delete the synthetic artifact so S3 and Postgres stay clean
  await fetch(`${PROD_BASE_URL}/api/v1/exports/${exportId}`, {
    method: 'DELETE',
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${CANARY_TOKEN}`,
      'x-canary-probe': 'true',
    },
  });

  console.log(`Canary probe passed in ${Date.now() - start}ms (exportId=${exportId})`);
}

runCanaryProbe().catch((err) => {
  console.error('CANARY_PROBE_FAILED:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});

Two consecutive failures from that page the on-call engineer trigger an automatic feature-flag kill-switch via webhook.

What We Still Test Before Production (No, We Didn't Delete Unit Tests)

Every time I tell someone we killed staging, they assume we just straight to and pray.

Not even close. We actually became about pre-merge checks in CI:

  • Every migration runs in an ephemeral Postgres container in GitHub Actions against a scrubbed schema snapshot, plus a lock-timeout check () so nobody accidentally locks for 45 minutes again.
  • Fast, deterministic, zero shared state. Runs in under 3 minutes per PR.
  • Frontend PRs still spin up a lightweight Vercel/preview build pointed at read-only mock or ephemeral backends for visual review—no shared database required.

What disappeared was the 4-hour human staging queue where nine engineers waited for one brittle cluster to unfreeze.

The Two Times Production Testing Bit Us

Moving verification to production is not free. Two mistakes in the first month taught us where the sharp edges are:

  1. Synthetic traffic leaked into an async billing job. Our API gateway filtered out from analytics, but the background SQS export worker did not read HTTP headers—it only saw the in the job payload. By Friday afternoon, had generated 43,200 fake export rows in our customer usage table. The fix was simple: we moved the synthetic marker into the JWT claims and tenant metadata () so every downstream worker and dbt model ignores it automatically.
  2. A column drop broke the 95% stable pods. During a canary rollout, old pods and new pods share the same Postgres database at the same time. Someone merged a PR that renamed to in a single migration. The 5% canary pods were happy; the 95% old pods immediately started throwing s. Now we enforce a strict two-PR rule in CI: PR #1 adds the new column and dual-writes, and PR #2 drops the old column only after 100% of pods are on the new version.
  3. A noisy third-party webhook masked a real canary regression. During a Monday afternoon Stripe retry storm, our canary spiked to 0.7% because of upstream s, triggering an unnecessary rollback on a harmless CSS/BFF deploy. We fixed that by splitting Prometheus queries into vs , and excluding known third-party upstream timeouts from the canary abort budget. Once we separated our own bugs from Stripe's hiccups, false-positive rollbacks dropped to near zero.

Six Months Without Staging: The Honest Scorecard

Shutting down our shared staging cluster was not magic. The first three weeks were bumpy—we had to train developers to wrap every risky change in a feature flag and add filtering to our billing reports so synthetic runs didn't inflate customer usage metrics.

Once that settled, though, the numbers spoke for themselves:

  • Monthly non-prod AWS bill: Dropped from to (ephemeral CI runners only).
  • Hotfix time-to-production: Cut from (waiting on staging locks and manual QA sign-off) to .
  • Customer-facing P1 outages: Dropped from 5 in the previous six months to (and Argo Rollouts auto-reverted that one at 5% traffic in 48 seconds before support even got a ticket).

If your staging environment costs thousands of dollars a month, blocks releases every Monday, and still lets real bugs slip into production, stop trying to make staging look more like production. It never will. Put your safety nets where the real traffic actually lives. Start with one non-critical service, wire up a 5% Argo canary with a two-metric Prometheus check, and see how fast your team stops missing Monday staging freezes.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

items.title: WiCi Infer Runs 800B-Parameter AI Models on a Laptop by Streaming Them From the SSD
items.author: sarahevans
items.content:
, the systems research lab behind the WiCi One wireless GPU, has released WiCi Infer, a free desktop app built to on a personal computer. It runs 800B-parameter models on Macs and Windows PCs that can hold only a fraction of the model in memory. Until now, running a model that size has meant owning more memory than any laptop ships with.

The app does not load the full model into RAM or GPU memory before it answers. It keeps the weights on the computer's SSD and pulls in the parts each step needs.

WiCi Infer is built on InferSSD, the open-source inference engine the company recently released. Both make the same argument: frontier AI should run on hardware people already own, without a data center behind it.

How Does WiCi Infer Run Large LLMs Locally With Limited Memory?

WiCi Infer stores the model on the SSD and moves only the active portion into memory as text is generated. That works because the models it targets are mixture-of-experts designs, which route each token through a small subset of their weights. Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, and about 42 billion are active at a time, according to WiCi.

InferSSD, which is built on llama.cpp, keeps those routed expert weights on disk. The shared layers, attention and working cache still have to fit in RAM or GPU memory, as WiCi explains in its write-up on running 800B-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware. Memory requirements shrink. They do not disappear.

That changes the hardware math for local AI. The files for an 800B-class model take up about 520GB, more than ten times the memory in a well-equipped laptop. With WiCi Infer, storage carries that load.

WiCi's published requirements:

  • DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (763B): 16GB of memory minimum, 48GB recommended
  • Muse Spark Open (816B): 24GB of memory minimum, 48GB recommended
  • Storage: about 520GB of available SSD space for either model
  • Platforms: macOS on Apple Silicon and Windows x64. Linux users run the InferSSD command-line engine.

Diagram showing WiCi Infer keeping about 520GB of model weights on the SSD and streaming active expert weights into RAM or GPU memory to generate tokens

How WiCi Infer runs an 800B-parameter model: weights stay on the SSD and only the active experts move into memory.

How Fast Are 800B-Parameter Models on Consumer Hardware?

WiCi's published benchmarks show about 2.7 tokens per second running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on an Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with 48GB of memory. Standard llama.cpp reached about 0.9 tokens per second on the same machine in WiCi's tests, which puts InferSSD at roughly three times the speed.

The same laptop produces about one token per second with Muse Spark Open, against 0.15 for llama.cpp.

Those speeds are slow next to smaller models or cloud AI services. At 2.7 tokens per second, a 300-word answer takes about two and a half minutes. The news is that models of this size run on a laptop at all.

The figures are WiCi's own, not independent tests. Results will vary with the computer, the model and the settings.

Bar chart of WiCi's published benchmarks on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro comparing InferSSD and llama.cpp tokens per second for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Spark Open

Decode speed on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, in tokens per second. Source: WiCi published benchmarks.

Yes, according to the company. WiCi Infer serves the loaded model through a local OpenAI-compatible API, so existing coding, writing and document tools can connect to a model running on the same machine. WiCi says prompts are processed locally, not on a cloud AI service, and the app requires no account or login.

For teams working with sensitive documents, source code or private business data, that is a practical reason to run a model locally. It also puts the choice of model, and where data is processed, in the user's hands.

The app has a graphical interface for downloading, launching and managing models, so no command line is required. The InferSSD engine underneath is open source, which lets developers inspect and build on it.

WiCi also makes WiCi One, a wireless GPU for local AI workloads. WiCi Infer applies the same idea in software: get more out of the hardware a person already has.

What Is the Trade-Off of Running Large AI Models Locally?

Large models have outgrown personal computers. Memory requirements climbed past what a desktop or laptop offers, which left cloud services as the practical option for most people.

WiCi Infer offers a second option by leaning on storage. The trade-off is plain: users need about 520GB of free SSD space, and generation is slow compared with the cloud. In return, an 800B-class model runs on a personal computer, privately, at no cost for the software.
